abstract: Environmental conditions experienced by parents can alter offspring phenotypes, with increasing evidence that parental cues have sex-specific intergenerational effects on sons and daughters. A key mechanistic step of such intergenerational plasticity involves the integration of parentally transmitted cues by early developing offspring through changes in gene regulatory processes. Sex-specific intergenerational effects may therefore arise if male and female embryos have divergent gene regulatory responses to shared parental cues - a process that could mitigate the severity of intersex conflicts associated with intergenerational inheritance. Using three-spine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus), we exposed fathers to predation risk and tested whether paternal cues are differentially integrated by male and female offspring by measuring gene regulatory responses across four stages spanning embryonic and early larval development. Consistent with sex-specific integration of parental cues, we found that paternal predation risk had sex-specific effects on gene expression across all stages of early development. Male gene expression responses to paternal predation risk were dominated by epigenetic processes, including DNA demethylation, whereas female responses were enriched for genes involved in transcriptional coregulation as well as neural and visual processes. ∼39% of genes responding to paternal predation cues in males were located on non-recombining regions of sex chromosomes, compared with only ∼1.6% of differentially reacting genes in females, suggesting that sex chromosome-associated genomic regions may contribute to sex-specific integration of shared parental cues. Altogether, our results demonstrate that sons and daughters integrate cues from fathers through distinct gene regulatory pathways, potentially facilitating the development and evolution of sex-specific phenotypes.
